full_judgment: 36. Probability of two views are possible in this case. The courts below convicted the accused (1) Israfil, (2) Abu Taher, (3) Alamgir, (4) Aminul Haque (5) Khorshida Begum and (6) Shamsunahar assuming that all of them, forming unlawful assembly with a common object to kill the victim, went to the place of occurrence and had killed the victim but we do not find any evidence either circumstantial or direct. There is no answer to the question as to who went to the place of occurrence and what was their actual number? All the members of the same family have been convicted relying only on presumption, surmises and conjectures. It is the cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence that a case can be said to be proved only when there is certain and explicit evidence and no person can be convicted on pure on moral conviction. Another golden thread which runs through the web of the administration of justice in criminal cases is that if two views are possible on the evidence adduced in the case, one pointing to the guilt of the accused and other to his, the view which favourable to the accused should be adopted innocence. This principle has a special relevance in cases wherein the guilt of the accused is sought to be established by circumstantial evidence. On consideration of the evidence and the circumstances referred to above, we are satisfied that this is a case in which the circumstantial evidence did not prove the case against accused conclusively and unerringly, and at any rate two reasonable views are possible.
